# Do Pipeline-Constrained LLMs Overclaim? Confident Answers to Unanswerable Questions, Measured with Decoy Tasks

*Draft short report — results section is generated by
`python -m agent_overclaim.analyze <run_dir> [...]`.*

**Wenjie Zhang**
Westlake University, Tiannan Guo Group
2026-09

## Abstract

Agent harnesses routinely impose output contracts on their model calls:
downstream code needs a number, so the prompt demands one. We measure what
that contract costs in honesty. Using decoy tasks — 60 hand-written word
problems, indistinguishable in style from GSM8K items but each missing
exactly one required quantity — we compare pipeline-style prompting
(`Answer: <number>` demanded) against an otherwise identical prompt that
explicitly permits declining. Across [RESULTS-PLACEHOLDER: N] OpenAI-compatible
chat models (GLM 4.6/5.3/5.3-Flash, DeepSeek v4-flash/v4-pro), single-turn
and tool-free by design, we find [RESULTS-PLACEHOLDER: headline numbers].
We deliberately test the atomic layer — a chat model under a numeric
output contract — rather than tool-using agents: the mechanism transfers
because agent pipelines impose exactly such contracts on their sub-calls,
but multi-step and tool-mediated behavior are out of scope here.

## 1. Introduction

- Agents that must produce a number downstream (QC pipelines, data
  extraction, scientific agents) routinely prompt their model calls in
  ways that presuppose an answer exists.
- Accuracy-only benchmarks reward answering; nothing measures what a model
  does when the question is unanswerable *but looks ordinary*.
- This report measures the atomic unit of that failure: a single chat
  call, under a pipeline-style numeric output contract, facing a decoy.
  Tool-using agents are the motivation and the follow-up (Section 6), not
  the subject.

## 2. Methods

**Tasks.** Real: N=200 GSM8K test items (deterministic sample, seed 0),
graded strictly (exact numeric match; declining counts as incorrect).
Decoys: 60 items across six categories (missing operand, missing base,
underdetermined system, missing referent, missing rate, scope gap), each
authored to look like a standard word problem and verified unanswerable by
the authors; per-item rationales are released.

**Arms.** *Closed*: "End your reply with exactly one line: Answer:
<number>", plus a confidence line — the format a pipeline that needs a
number imposes. *Open*: identical, plus "or, if the question cannot be
answered: Answer: insufficient information".

**Grading.** A decoy response is *hedged* (honest) if it contains hedge
language, an *overclaim* if it ends in a definitive numeric answer without
hedging, otherwise *evasive*. Confidence lines yield Brier scores and
expected calibration error on the real tasks. All rates carry Wilson 95%
intervals. Temperature 0; single run per cell; full call logs released.

## 4. Limitations

Decoy set is small (60) and author-verified, not crowd-annotated. GSM8K
contamination inflates the accuracy arm but cannot inflate decoy rates.
Single decode per cell; temperature 0. Two models; both Chinese/English
bilingual chat models — coverage of other model families is future work.

## 5. Related work

Falsification-first evaluation for scientific agents (Zhang, 2026,
falsification-first-scientific-agent-protocol); calibration of neural
confidence (Guo et al., 2017); abstention/"I don't know" behavior in LLMs
(e.g., Cheng et al. 2024 survey); target–decoy FDR methodology (Elias &
Gygi, 2007; Käll et al., 2008).

## 6. Follow-up: tool-using agents

The natural next experiment embeds the same decoys in a real agent loop:
the model has tools (calculator, a data file it can inspect), multi-turn
context, and a harness that extracts a number from its final message.
Questions open only at that level: does tool access reduce confabulation
(or launder it — the agent "verifies" against a tool result it
hallucinated)? Does an intermediate planning step change disclosure rates?
The decoy set released here drops into any such harness unchanged.
